title: five disguises, one promise
hookLine: the forest years are over, and to keep their word, five brothers and Draupadi must vanish for a year
carry: satya: keep your word, even when it humbles you

cards: One last year, lived among people, without being recognized. Those were the terms of the dice game, and if anyone sees through them, the exile begins again.
So the five brothers and Draupadi sit together, and Yudhishthira asks each of them a question. Not where will you hide. What will you be?

Where will you work, and as whom? They have chosen a kingdom to vanish into: the land of the Matsyas, ruled by King Virata. The Virata book opens with something close to a job interview, held in secret.

teach.b: Why go through with it at all? In the forest, Bhima begged Yudhishthira more than once to stop waiting and fight; the dice game was rigged. And Yudhishthira said no.

teach.h: KEPT PROMISES, AND KANKA THE DICER.
teach.b: That's the teaching under this whole year, and Hindus have a word for it: satya, truth, which includes the promise kept.

In the stories Hindu families grow up on, King Harishchandra gives up his kingdom rather than break his word, and Rama goes to the forest so his father's promise stands. The Pandavas belong to that line.
So listen to the answers. Yudhishthira will be Kanka, a Brahmin who plays dice with the king. The man whose love of dice cost them everything wears it as his cover.

teach.h: A COOK, A DANCE TEACHER, A MAID.
teach.b: Bhima will be Vallava, the cook. Arjuna will hide his bowstring scars under bangles and live as Brihannala, who teaches dance to the palace women. Nakula will keep the horses, Sahadeva the cattle.
And Draupadi, a queen, will serve a queen as Sairandhri, a maid who dresses hair.
Their priest Dhaumya gives them rules for a king's house: don't take a seat that might be someone else's, speak when you're asked, don't show off.

Princes become staff for a year, to keep a promise made to people who cheated them. Today, satya rarely costs a throne. It looks like the promise you made when it was easy, kept when it's embarrassing.
In Hindu teaching, a word given is part of dharma.

how: Retellings of the Virata book keep the disguise names (Kanka, Vallava, Brihannala, Sairandhri), and the year in hiding is told as a promise kept to the letter; Harishchandra and Rama are the stories Hindu families most often tell about keeping one's word.

o: the forest where the Pandavas spent their exile
the king of the Matsyas, where the Pandavas hide
the queen's brother, who commands the army

games.q: who hid as whom? tap the pairs.
p: Yudhishthira, playing dice with the king

s: the year in hiding was a punishment Dharma gave them at the lake
it was the term they agreed to at the dice game; Dharma only promised no one would know them.
Arjuna hid his bowstring scars under bangles
he lived as Brihannala, teaching song and dance in the palace.
Yudhishthira could have fought early, but kept the dice-game terms
Bhima urged him to fight; he said he had given his word.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. you were cheated at dice, and Bhima says fight now instead of hiding for a year. what does satya ask?
o: fight. a cheater's terms don't count.
keep the year you agreed to, even as a servant.
hide, but quietly break the terms if no one's looking.
games.why: he keeps his word. in Hindu teaching satya, truth and the promise kept, is part of dharma, even when the other side cheated.

practice: Hindus often begin a puja or a vow with a sankalpa, a stated resolve. Choose one small promise you can truly keep today, something you already owe someone. Some hold a little water in the right palm as they say it.
Say it once, silently and plainly, and stay with it for a few breaths. If you pray, you can make it in your prayer; if you don't, simply say it to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Virata. The king of the Matsyas, whose court will hide the Pandavas and Draupadi for their year in disguise.

orig.note: the king of the Matsyas; his name titles this book of the epic, the Virata Parva.

carryVoice: Your line: satya, keep your word, even when it humbles you. A dice player, a cook, a dance teacher, two herders and a maid. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Pandava-pravesa), the Pandavas choose their disguises and Dhaumya's counsel on living in a king's household
Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Bhima urges Yudhishthira to fight before the term ends, and Yudhishthira refuses because of his pledge
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda: Rama goes to the forest so Dasharatha's promise to Kaikeyi stands
Markandeya Purana, the story of Harishchandra, who gives up his kingdom to keep his word
